II. ANALYSIS 
 Mr. Smith argues, among other things, that the Board failed to provide adequate reasons or 
bases for its rationale that his December 2019 claim for major depression and anxiety disorder did 
not encompass an earlier claim for PTSD. Appellant's Brief (Br.) at 8-18 (citing Clemons, 
23 Vet.App. at 5-6). The Secretary contends that the claim before the Board was the February 2020 
RO rating decision granting service connection for MDD and anxious distress effective December 
18, 2019, that was appealed in March 2020 and where Mr. Smith elected the direct review docket. 
Secretary's Br. at 9. As with any finding on a material issue of fact and law presented on the record, the Board must support its 
effective-date determination with adequate reasons or bases that enable the claimant to understand 
the precise basis for that determination and facilitate review in this Court. See 38 U.S.C. 
§ 7104(d)(1); Gilbert v. Derwinski, 1 Vet.App. 49, 56-57 (1990). 
 The Board's failure to address the Clemons issue raised by the record — that Mr. Smith's December 2019 claim for major depression and anxiety disorder reasonably encompassed an earlier 2009 PTSD claim — leaves this Court without the means to perform meaningful review of the effective-date determination. On remand, the Board must address whether Mr. Smith's prior 2009 filing constitutes a pending and unadjudicated claim and provide adequate reasons or bases for its conclusion.

Although Mr. Barber objects to the 2011 examiner's conclusions, he fails to demonstrate 
that the examiner lacked the competence to make them. Examiners who "offer[] medical opinions 
in veterans benefits cases are nothing more or less than expert witnesses." Nieves-Rodriguez v. 
Peake, 22 Vet.App. 295, 302 (2008). The Board utilizes their opinions to inform its decision on 
medical matters. See Colvin v. Derwinski, 1 Vet.App. 171, 172 (1990) (Board "must consider only 
independent medical evidence to support their findings rather than provide their own medical 
judgment in the guise of a Board opinion"). The 2011 examiner's opinion that the veteran was 
malingering was based on the results of psychological and medical tests that the examiner 
interpreted based on his professional education and experience. These are medical conclusions that 
fall within the examiner's area of expertise, and the Board did not err in relying on these medical 
conclusions or in according them probative weight. See id. 
 Mr. Barber also argues that the Board erred in according little probative weight to the 
medical examinations that diagnosed PTSD. The Board explained that it discounted the 
examinations because they "are based on [the veteran's] self-reported statements to the medical 
providers, which the Board deems are not credible." R. at 19. The Court discerns no error in the 
Board's explanation or weighing of the evidence. A medical examination that is based on an 
inaccurate factual premise lacks probative value. Reonal v. Brown, 5 Vet.App. 458, 461 (1993).

Having cleared away this initial point, the Court turns to the merits. As mentioned above, 
appellant asserts that the April 2009 and February 2015 examination reports are inadequate. When 
the Secretary elects to provide a medical examination, that examination must be adequate. Barr v. 
Nicholson, 21 Vet.App. 303, 311-12 (2007); see Stegall v. West, 11 Vet.App. 268, 270-71 (1998) 
(remanding where a VA examination was "inadequate for evaluation purposes"). A medical 
examination is adequate "where it is based upon consideration of the veteran's prior medical history 
and examination and also describes the disability . . . in sufficient detail so that the Board's 
'evaluation of the claimed disability will be a fully informed one.'" Stefl v. Nicholson, 21 Vet.App. 
120, 123 (2007) (quoting Ardison v. Brown, 6 Vet.App. 405, 407 (1994)). In the end, "[t]he Board 
must be able to conclude that a medical expert has applied valid medical analysis to the significant 
facts of the particular case in order to reach the conclusions submitted in a medical opinion." 
Nieves-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet.App. 295, 301 (2008). 
 The Court reviews the Board's determination that a medical examination is adequate under 
the clearly erroneous standard of review. D'Aries v. Peake, 22 Vet.App. 97, 104 (2008). On this record, the Court is left with the definite and firm conviction that the April 2009 examiner did not address the lay history of in-service back pain and that the February 2015 examination report incorporated the deficiencies of the earlier examination. Because the Board's prior June 2013 remand order specifically directed the RO to obtain an examination addressing the lay history, the Board's reliance on these inadequate examinations also constitutes a failure to ensure substantial compliance with the remand order. See Stegall, 11 Vet.App. at 271. Vacatur and remand are required.
